360.bp: Web services increasingly rely on nearby machines, not only distant cloud centers. A base station, roadside server, or small local data center can answer requests faster because it sits close to users and devices. Drones and other end devices may also collect the freshest data, but they are weaker, battery-limited, and often cannot hand over raw records because the connection is long, slow, or privacy rules forbid it. This paper serves that practical setting: train useful models on both sides, edge servers and end devices, while sending much less information than full data or full models. The problem is not just speed. The abstract says existing collaborative learning often assumes the server and device use the same model shape, while real deployments may use different model sizes and designs. PAECL treats collaboration as exchanging compact class summaries, called prototypes, so heterogeneous models can still teach each other.
360.wh: The hard part is that the two sides need each other for different reasons. End devices have the real examples, because drones or phones observe the world directly. Edge servers have more stable computing power and can reduce service latency once their models are trained. But the edge server may have no timely access to device data, either because the device is far away or because privacy regulations keep raw data local. A simple collaborative system would send model weights, raw examples, or per-example output scores, but the abstract says those choices create substantial transmission overhead. The mismatch between edge and end models adds another difficulty: if the server and device have different internal shapes, sharing a whole model or directly matching every output can be awkward. The central tension is therefore communication versus knowledge: the system must move enough signal for training while refusing to move the heavy or private objects that would make training easy.
360.naive: A smart beginner might ask every drone or device to upload its training data to the edge server, train a strong edge model there, and send updated guidance back. That fails when distance delays the upload or privacy rules block it. Another attempt is to keep data local but share complete model updates, as in many distributed training systems. That can still be too expensive when devices and servers communicate repeatedly under limited training resources. A third attempt is to require the same model architecture everywhere, so updates line up neatly. The abstract says existing approaches often make this isomorphic-model assumption, but edge servers and end devices may need different model forms. These simple plans fail because they move the wrong thing: too much private detail, too many parameters, or a model shape that both sides cannot share.
360.ap: The paper's central move is to send class-wise feature vectors, called prototypes, instead of sending data, full models, or logits. A prototype is a compact numerical summary of what examples from one class tend to look like inside a device's model; it is not the raw image, sensor record, or user event itself. PAECL then augments these prototypes, meaning it creates useful variations of the class summaries so they can carry more training signal than a single average-like point. On end devices, the method strengthens prototype knowledge through local prototype contrast and global prototype alignment: local summaries are made more distinct from other local classes, while summaries from different participants are lined up so the same class has a shared meaning. On edge servers, prototypes are mixed with random noise to produce bounded virtual vectors, which are fed to generative models to supply training material when the server has no raw device data.
360.mech: The mechanism begins with end devices training on their own local data. Each device turns examples into internal feature vectors, which are lists of numbers summarizing what the model has noticed after compressing the raw input. For each class, the device forms a prototype, a class-level summary vector. Instead of uploading its records or the whole local model, the device transmits these augmented class summaries. Before or during that transmission, PAECL improves the summaries in two ways. Local prototype contrast compares class summaries inside the same device and pushes the training signal to preserve differences between classes, so a drone's summary for one class does not collapse into another. Global prototype alignment then makes prototypes for the same class agree across participating devices, so the edge server receives a shared class language rather than many incompatible private dialects. At the edge server, there is no local device data to train on. The server therefore further augments the received prototypes by mixing them with random noise while keeping the resulting vectors bounded. These bounded virtual vectors are passed into generative models, which produce data-like training signal for the edge model. The output is simultaneous training of heterogeneous end and edge models with less communication than sharing models, data, or per-example score lists.
360.math: The main mathematical idea is controlled compression. Raw examples are too large or too private to move, so each class is represented by a prototype: a point in a feature-vector space, where nearby points are supposed to mean similar class evidence and separated points are supposed to mean different classes. This is a similarity idea, but with a tradeoff. A prototype preserves the central class signal and loses individual detail; that is useful for privacy and bandwidth, but it can hide rare cases. Local prototype contrast is comparison-based learning: it asks the model to treat the right class summary as close and competing class summaries as farther away. Global prototype alignment is a consistency constraint: summaries created by different devices should name the same class in a compatible way, even if their local models differ. The edge-side noise mixing uses controlled randomness. Random noise creates variation around the class summary, while bounds keep the virtual vectors from wandering into meaningless regions. The generative model then maps these vectors into training material for the edge model. The math fits because the problem is about moving a small useful signal across a costly, privacy-sensitive boundary.
360.dots: In the repo's current taxonomy, this paper belongs with Privacy, Federated and Security work because the raw data stays on end devices while useful training signal crosses the boundary. It also connects to Efficiency and Scalability because the scarce resource is communication: the abstract explicitly contrasts prototypes with sharing models, data, or logits. A neighboring idea is learning from examples, where a system reuses patterns from past cases without writing hand rules; here the reusable pattern is compressed into class prototypes. It also sits near recommendation, graph, and retrieval papers that use similarity: many conference papers turn messy objects into compact vectors, compare closeness, and train from those comparisons. PAECL's surface vocabulary is edge-end collaborative learning, but its deeper problem is shared with federated learning papers: many parties hold different evidence, cannot pool it directly, and need a smaller common language for cooperation.
360.ww: The approach should improve over the naive solutions because it matches the actual bottleneck. If raw device data cannot arrive at the edge server on time, then a method that depends on raw upload is fragile from the start. If full models or per-example score lists are expensive to transmit, then collaboration must use a smaller object. Class prototypes are small enough to communicate repeatedly and meaningful enough to guide training. The local contrast step helps because a prototype is only useful if it marks class differences, not just class averages blurred together. The global alignment step helps because heterogeneous devices can otherwise produce summaries that point in incompatible directions; alignment makes the summaries usable as a shared teaching signal. The edge-side augmentation matters because a server with no data would otherwise train on too few points. Mixing prototypes with bounded random variation gives the generative model a controlled neighborhood around each class summary, producing richer training signal without pretending the server saw the original private data.
360.po: The payoff is practical collaborative training for web applications that depend on nearby edge service. The abstract claims PAECL simultaneously trains heterogeneous edge and end models even when edge servers lack data from end devices. It reduces communication overhead by sending augmented class-wise feature vectors rather than full data, full models, or logits. The reported simulations and field experiments show the highest accuracy for both edge and end models under limited training resources, though the provided abstract cuts off before giving the full final wording or numerical results.
360.limits: Several assumptions must hold. Prototypes must preserve enough class information for training; if a class has many rare subtypes, one summary may erase important cases. The method also assumes prototype sharing is acceptable under the relevant privacy rules, even though prototypes can still reveal some aggregate class information. Global alignment depends on different devices agreeing enough about class meaning. Edge-side virtual vectors are only useful if bounded noise and the generative model create plausible training signal rather than misleading artificial cases. The abstract reports simulations and field experiments, but it does not provide dataset details, privacy leakage analysis, communication numbers, or failure cases in this input.

361.bp: Urban planning is the work of deciding what kinds of city functions belong where: housing, business, public services, green space, transportation support, and other land uses that shape daily life. The paper starts from a practical pressure: good plans affect residents' quality of life, social stability, and sustainable city development, but making them is slow when experts must manually examine maps, population needs, and competing preferences. A purely automatic planner can be faster, yet it often shuts out the people who will live with the result. Intelli-Planner tries to make plan generation both customized and participatory. Its inputs are demographic data, geographic data, and planning preferences. From those, it estimates high-level planning requirements and demand for each functional type, then uses a learning system to generate planning schemes. The ordinary goal is not simply to draw a nicer map. It is to turn local facts and stakeholder wishes into city-layout decisions that can be scored from several angles.
361.wh: The hard part is that a city plan is not one decision. Each placement changes the value of later placements, because a school, park, commercial district, or residential area matters partly through its neighbors and through the people it serves. A human expert can reason about such tradeoffs, but expert-led planning is time-consuming and labor-intensive. A standard data-driven method can search faster, but the abstract says these methods often limit stakeholder involvement, so the plan may score well on technical measures while failing the people whose preferences define success. The tension is therefore double: the system must handle a large choice space and must preserve human-facing preference information. It also must balance objective metrics with satisfaction, which may not point in the same direction. A plan that looks efficient by one measure can still feel wrong if it ignores local demand, demographic differences, or competing views about what a neighborhood should become.
361.naive: A smart beginner might collect demographic and geographic tables, write rules for each land-use type, and place functions wherever the rules give the highest score. For example, put public services near dense populations, put green space where land is available, and keep incompatible functions apart. This is understandable because planning seems like matching needs to locations. It fails because rules become brittle as soon as preferences conflict or the city setting changes. Another beginner might ask experts to review every candidate plan, but that restores the original cost and delay. A third attempt is to train a plain prediction model from past plans, but that can copy old patterns without letting stakeholders shape the new plan. The missing piece is a feedback loop where candidate plans are tried, scored, and improved.
361.ap: The paper's central move is to combine two kinds of machinery. The first is a language model, a system trained to work with ordinary written instructions and descriptions, used here to help represent planning preferences and stakeholder judgments. The second is deep reinforcement learning, meaning a learner that chooses actions, receives scores, and gradually changes its policy so future actions receive better scores. Intelli-Planner uses demographic data, geographic data, and preferences to infer high-level requirements and demands for each functional type. Then a policy network, the part that chooses planning actions, is trained with extra knowledge enhancement so its choices are not guided only by raw trial and error. The generated schemes are judged through a multi-dimensional evaluation system, including satisfaction scores from LLM-based stakeholders. In concrete terms, the system turns city facts and preferences into candidate plans, tests them against several kinds of feedback, and updates the planner toward schemes that satisfy both measured planning goals and stakeholder-like evaluations.
361.mech: The mechanism begins with a description of an urban setting: who lives there, what the geography looks like, and what planning preferences have been stated. Intelli-Planner first uses this information to form high-level planning requirements. Instead of treating every land-use decision as isolated, it estimates the demand for each functional type, so the planner has a sense of how much of each kind of city function is needed. Those requirements become the state seen by the decision-making policy network. The policy then proposes planning actions, which can be understood as choices that gradually build a planning scheme. During training, a knowledge enhancement module supplies additional planning-relevant guidance to improve the policy network's decisions; the abstract does not specify the exact knowledge source, so the safe claim is that it augments the learner beyond raw reward signals. Each generated scheme is evaluated by a multi-dimensional system. Some dimensions are objective planning metrics, and another source of feedback comes from LLM-based stakeholders that assign satisfaction scores. The reinforcement-learning loop then treats those evaluations as signals about which choices were helpful. Over repeated training, the policy changes so it reaches useful plans faster, which the abstract describes as improved convergence speed. The final output is a customized planning scheme rather than a single universal template.
361.math: The main mathematical idea is sequential choice under feedback. A city plan can be viewed as a long path through many possible choices, where each step changes the remaining possibilities. Reinforcement learning is the plain-language idea of learning from consequences: the policy chooses an action, the evaluator scores what happened, and the policy is adjusted so actions leading to better scores become more likely. The policy network is the adjustable rule for choosing actions. The evaluation system defines what better means, which is crucial because a learner will chase the score it is given. Here the score is multi-dimensional, so the math must compare plans across several kinds of value rather than one simple number. That fits urban planning because livability, functional demand, objective layout quality, and satisfaction are different pressures. There is also an optimization idea: optimization means defining a target and searching the space of possible settings or choices for plans that improve that target. The repo's optimization concept links urban planning to other papers where a large choice space is too big for hand rules, so feedback guides search. The tradeoff is measurement versus meaning: scores make search possible, but only if they faithfully stand in for the planning values people care about.
361.dots: This paper belongs with the conference's reinforcement-learning family because it treats planning as a feedback-guided sequence of decisions, not as a one-shot prediction. The repo's reinforcement-learning manifest includes many papers where an agent must act under changing or costly conditions, such as crawling dynamic data sources, allocating advertising budgets, choosing tools, or steering attacks and defenses. Intelli-Planner uses the same deeper pattern in a city setting: many choices are possible, direct hand-design is expensive, and feedback tells the system which direction is better. It also connects to the neighboring Lang2Plan paper in the same batch, which uses language models and interactive 3D editing for building layout planning. Both papers use language models to lower the expertise barrier in spatial design, but Intelli-Planner emphasizes urban-scale planning schemes, reinforcement-learning training, and stakeholder satisfaction scoring. It also sits near broader themes of optimization, simulation, and participatory AI, where technical scores must be balanced against human-facing preferences.
361.ww: The approach should improve over the naive rule-based planner because it does not have to freeze planning knowledge into a fixed checklist. If two urban settings differ in population, geography, or stated preferences, the input requirements and functional demands can differ too, so the policy is trained to respond to context. It should also improve over a purely expert-driven process in speed, because the trained policy can generate candidate schemes without starting every case from scratch. The satisfaction-scoring part matters because it gives the learner a route to include stakeholder-like feedback during training rather than only after a plan is finished. The knowledge enhancement module matters for a different reason: raw trial and error in a large planning space can waste many attempts, while added knowledge can bias the policy toward choices that make planning sense. The abstract's reported convergence speed supports this interpretation. The deeper reason is that the method gives the planner repeated, structured feedback from several evaluators, so it can learn which planning actions tend to produce schemes that are both objectively acceptable and more satisfying.
361.po: The payoff is a planning generator that can produce customized urban schemes from demographic data, geographic data, and preferences while keeping stakeholder satisfaction visible in the training loop. The abstract says experiments across diverse urban settings show performance above traditional baselines, comparable objective metrics to state-of-the-art deep-reinforcement-learning methods, higher stakeholder satisfaction, and faster convergence. In practical terms, this buys planners a faster way to create candidate plans that are not only technically scored but also checked against simulated stakeholder responses. That does not replace public planning judgment, but it can shift expert effort from manually constructing every option toward inspecting, correcting, and choosing among better-prepared alternatives.
361.limits: Several assumptions must hold. The demographic and geographic data must describe the city well enough for high-level requirements to be meaningful. The planning preferences must be collected and represented in a way that does not erase minority or conflicting views. The LLM-based stakeholders must be credible stand-ins for real stakeholder satisfaction; the abstract reports satisfaction scoring but does not prove that simulated stakeholders match actual residents, officials, or businesses. The multi-dimensional evaluation system must weight its criteria responsibly, because the learner will optimize what is scored. The abstract also does not specify the exact planning actions, knowledge enhancement content, or deployment setting, so claims about real-world adoption should stay cautious.

362.bp: This paper is about reading emotion from a moving human face while also listening to the sound that comes with it. The real system might be a social-media analyzer, a meeting assistant, or an interactive agent that needs to notice whether a person looks happy, angry, afraid, neutral, or uncertain over time. Video alone is incomplete: a smile can be polite, a face can be partly hidden, and the strongest clue may be in the rhythm or tone of speech. Audio alone is also incomplete because sound does not show eyebrow movement, mouth shape, gaze, or the timing of an expression. Dynamic facial expression recognition therefore becomes a translation problem between two changing streams. BHGap tries to make the listening side and the watching side guide each other throughout processing, instead of waiting until both have already formed separate opinions.
362.wh: The hard part is that audio and video are not two copies of the same signal. A video stream is made of changing visual patterns across face regions and frames. An audio stream is made of changing sound patterns over time. They may describe the same emotion, but their internal shapes are different, and they may peak at different moments. Existing approaches, according to the abstract, often join the two streams in a shallow and static way. That means the system lets each side build its own description and then combines them once, as if their relationship were fixed. This misses co-evolution: an audio clue might tell the visual reader which facial motion matters, while a visual clue might tell the audio reader which tone change is expressive. The second difficulty is alignment. If the two streams live in different feature distributions, a rough final match can leave them speaking mismatched internal languages.
362.naive: A smart beginner would train one video model, train one audio model, take their final outputs or feature vectors, and concatenate them before classification. This is attractive because it is simple: watch, listen, glue the results together, then predict the expression. It fails when the useful relation is not at the end but throughout the interpretation process. Early visual layers may capture mouth motion, later layers may capture expression meaning, and the audio stream may need to guide both. A one-shot join cannot repair mismatches that have already accumulated inside the separate encoders. It also treats alignment as a single coarse act, even though global timing agreement and fine semantic agreement are different problems.
362.ap: BHGap's central move is to turn audio-visual collaboration from a late merge into a continuing conversation between the two streams. The abstract says the method uses frozen backbone encoders, meaning large pre-existing readers whose main settings are kept fixed. At every encoding layer, a State Space Model based cross-modal prompt generator produces guidance prompts for the other modality. In plain terms, the audio side sends a small steering signal to the visual side, and the visual side sends a steering signal back, layer after layer. After this deep reciprocal prompting, the paper adds multi-stage alignment. At a macro level, it uses a compressed adversarial alignment step to reduce broad audio-video distribution gaps and encourage spatio-temporal congruity. At a micro level, it uses Maximum Mean Discrepancy constraints with implicit-differentiation optimization to make finer statistical and semantic matches.
362.mech: The input is a paired audio-video clip for dynamic facial expression recognition. One frozen encoder processes the visual stream, and another frozen encoder processes the audio stream. At a given layer, each encoder has an intermediate description of its stream: not the raw pixels or sound anymore, but a structured set of signals about what it has noticed so far. BHGap feeds those intermediate descriptions into a cross-modal prompt generator built around a State Space Model, a sequence machine designed to keep track of changing state over time. The generator creates a guidance prompt for the opposite stream. The visual encoder receives audio-guided hints, and the audio encoder receives video-guided hints, so the next layer is influenced by what the other side currently knows. This repeats across layers, making the two descriptions change together rather than separately. After encoding, the system aligns the resulting audio and video features in stages. The macro stage tries to make the broad spatio-temporal structures compatible and reduce global distribution differences, using low-rank adversarial alignment: a compressed matching game where one part tries to expose modality differences and the encoder-side representation is pushed to hide irrelevant modality gaps. The micro stage applies Maximum Mean Discrepancy constraints and implicit differentiation optimization so fine-grained statistics and semantic meanings line up before the final fusion and expression prediction.
362.math: The main mathematical ideas are sequence state, guided weighting, distribution matching, compressed structure, and optimization. A State Space Model can be understood as a way to summarize a changing stream by carrying a memory of what has happened and updating that memory as new evidence arrives. That fits audio-video emotion recognition because expressions unfold over time; a raised voice or widening eyes matters partly because of when it appears. The guidance prompt is a learned steering signal, close to weighted focus: it tells the counterpart encoder which parts of its current representation should matter more now. Low-rank alignment means using a compressed form that keeps the main shared pattern while avoiding the cost and noise of matching every possible detail. Adversarial alignment is a matching game: if a critic can easily tell audio features from video features, the representations are still too modality-specific; if it cannot, broad gaps have been reduced. Maximum Mean Discrepancy is a statistical comparison between two groups of features. It asks whether their average behavior, under a chosen notion of similarity, looks alike. Implicit differentiation optimization means choosing settings through a nested learning problem without manually unrolling every internal adjustment. The tradeoff is alignment versus over-forcing: the streams should agree where emotion is shared, but not erase useful modality-specific evidence.
362.dots: This paper sits inside the repo's multimodal vision-language and multimodal expression-recognition thread, where the recurring difficulty is not just having many data types but deciding how their evidence should influence one another. It connects to sequence modeling because emotion is dynamic: the order and timing of face and voice changes matter. It connects to attention-like ideas because prompts act as learned guidance about what should receive more influence, though the paper's abstract frames this through cross-modal prompting rather than a simple focus layer. It also connects to statistical alignment papers across recommendation, retrieval, and multimodal learning: many conference systems face the same problem of two evidence sources describing one object in incompatible internal coordinates. BHGap's surface task is facial expression recognition, but the deeper conference problem is controlled fusion: how to let separate signals cooperate without letting one noisy or mismatched channel dominate.
362.ww: The mechanism should work better than late fusion because it gives each stream corrective information before its interpretation has hardened. If the visual stream sees mouth movement but is uncertain whether it is speech, laughter, or tension, audio guidance can change which visual cues are emphasized in the next layer. If the audio stream hears a tone change but needs facial timing to distinguish excitement from anger, visual guidance can steer the sound interpretation. Repeating this across layers matters because early, middle, and late features describe different levels of the event. The macro alignment step then reduces broad mismatch between audio and video feature populations, so fusion is not trying to combine signals that still live in separate coordinate systems. The micro alignment step addresses smaller statistical and semantic differences that broad matching can miss. The intuitive gain is that collaboration and alignment happen at the same depth as the representation is being built, not only after both streams have already made incompatible summaries.
362.po: The payoff is a more deliberate audio-visual emotion recognizer for dynamic facial expression recognition. The abstract reports extensive experiments on the public DFEW and MAFW datasets and says BHGap achieves state-of-the-art performance. More importantly, the claimed capability is specific: the system can use audio and video as mutually guiding streams across frozen encoders, then align their outputs at coarse and fine levels before fusion. In practical terms, this buys a better chance of recognizing expressions in clips where neither face motion nor voice alone gives a stable answer.
362.limits: The claims depend on the assumption that audio and video carry complementary emotion evidence and are paired well enough for cross-modal guidance to help. If one modality is missing, badly corrupted, weakly related to the expression, or socially misleading, reciprocal prompting may spread noise rather than clarity. The abstract names DFEW and MAFW experiments but does not prove performance for every culture, camera setting, language, microphone condition, age group, or social context. It also does not show from the abstract alone how interpretable the prompts are, how expensive the multi-stage alignment is, or when alignment might erase useful differences between face and voice.

363.bp: Recommendation systems suggest products or content by finding similar users or items. Most use graph structures (users connected to items they rated), but whether those graphs actually flow information well—whether they have good connectivity—was barely studied.
363.wh: Graphs can have bottlenecks: clusters of users weakly connected to other clusters, like islands. A graph with poor connectivity ('weak' in mathematical terms) means that a user's information can't flow far, so recommendations stay local and miss relevant items. Existing systems treat the graph as given and fixed.
363.ap: The system identifies which edges (connections) are bottlenecks by analyzing the graph's mathematical structure. Then it learns to re-weight those edges—making bottleneck connections stronger while leaving good ones alone. A lightweight neural network makes these weight adjustments guided by a mathematical constraint that encourages overall connectivity.
363.ww: Strong connectivity means any user's taste can influence any item's score. By fixing bottleneck edges, information flows faster and farther, so the system sees the full picture of user interests rather than siloed neighborhoods.
363.po: Recommendation accuracy improves significantly, especially for harder recommendation scenarios, by making the underlying graph structure more connected.

364.bp: AI systems now power ranking, recommendations, ads—most of what people see online. But if someone asks 'why did this appear?' there's often no answer. Imagine a receipt for every recommendation: what data was used, which model version, who checked it. That's the vision.
364.wh: Platforms treat AI decisions as black boxes for competitive and privacy reasons. There's no standard way to prove a model version is what actually ran, no audit trail of which data went in, no way for third parties to verify the system wasn't gamed.
364.ap: The system creates a decentralized transparency log (inspired by certificate transparency for HTTPS). Every inference generates a cryptographic receipt proving what model ran, what data was used, and what came out. These receipts get logged in a append-only ledger anyone can verify. Model metadata and lineage get registered and signed so switching versions is traceable.
364.ww: Cryptographic receipts are tiny (logarithmic in the number of inferences). Their verification cost is microseconds per request. The decentralized log means no single company controls the audit trail, making tampering visible to everyone.
364.po: Platforms can offer third-party auditing and transparency without leaking proprietary details, enabling regulatory compliance and public accountability for AI-mediated platforms.

365.bp: Hateful memes are dangerous because the meaning comes from the combo of image and text—neither alone tells the story. But in practice images break (media links die), text gets corrupted, or data gets lost upstream. A deployed system needs to work anyway, not crash or fall back to separate models.
365.wh: Fusion models (systems that combine modalities) are often brittle—they expect all inputs to be perfect. If an image is missing, standard approaches fail. Building a separate fallback system for each missing-modality case is expensive and error-prone.
365.ap: Instead of fusing modalities at the end, project both image and text into a shared safety space (a learned representation everyone understands) using frozen pre-trained encoders plus tiny learned adapters. Then feed whatever modalities are available to a single classifier, always in the same way.
365.ww: A shared space means the classifier speaks one language. Missing a modality is just an empty slot in an aggregation function—the system naturally handles it. Frozen encoders keep parameters small; only projectors are trained.
365.po: System matches fusion-only performance with all modalities present while gracefully handling missing images or text without retraining or fallback logic, matching specialized single-modality models when needed.

366.bp: Professional architects spend days on floor plans, constrained by codes and aesthetics. What if a designer could describe what they want in natural language and get multiple interactive 3D options to refine, each photorealistic and spatially correct?
366.wh: Language is ambiguous ('make it open' could mean open-plan or glass walls). Simple text-to-layout methods demand very formal, precise input. They also can't let users tweak designs mid-process, and 2D floor plans don't let you visualize or immerse yourself in the space.
366.ap: A multi-agent LLM system breaks the language description into sub-tasks (identify room types, set constraints, place fixtures). A web-based 3D editor lets users adjust the intermediate design and see feedback before rendering. Finally, a diffusion model with spatial controls generates photorealistic 3D renderings from chosen viewpoints.
366.ww: Breaking language into sub-tasks makes it robust to vague input. Interactive 3D editing lets the user steer the system when it misunderstands. Photorealistic rendering (rather than abstract plans) helps users visualize and trust the design.
366.po: System generates buildable layouts from conversational input, with immersive 3D renderings and full user control over intermediate design decisions.

367.bp: Legal AI research is exploding—models analyzing contracts, predicting case outcomes, writing briefs. But there's no standard way to evaluate these systems. Each lab uses different benchmarks and metrics, making it hard to compare progress or spot which methods actually help lawyers.
367.wh: Legal tasks are diverse (document classification, Q&A, contract review, case prediction) with different performance measures. A single framework has to handle this variety, run efficiently, and let researchers easily add new tasks without breaking existing ones.
367.ap: LegalKit is a toolkit that integrates many legal benchmarks into one system with a shared configuration interface and web UI. It supports different acceleration backends (to run on different hardware) and checkpoints let you pause and resume experiments mid-way.
367.ww: Unified infrastructure means researchers compare apples-to-apples. Web UI lowers barriers for non-ML experts. Checkpoint recovery matters for long legal evaluations. Modularity means new benchmarks slot in easily without redesigning the whole pipeline.
367.po: Legal NLP research becomes reproducible and comparable across studies; researchers can focus on novel methods instead of building evaluation infrastructure from scratch.

368.bp: Starlink satellites now outnumber all other satellites combined and beam internet to millions. Yet nobody outside SpaceX knows much about its internal network structure, where traffic flows, or what services are exposed. Transparency matters for security and policy.
368.wh: Starlink keeps internal details private, and direct access to their systems is restricted. You can't just call them and ask 'how does your routing work.' But DNS records leak hints—servers accidentally reveal internal structure—and you can scan public IP ranges to spot patterns.
368.ap: By analyzing leaked DNS data, researchers infer how Starlink's internal networks split into zones and what services sit where. Passive DNS shows user behavior (which services people use, traffic patterns). Active scanning of public IPs reveals which services are exposed and whether they have security holes.
368.ww: DNS is a side channel—DNS servers sometimes leak the topology accidentally. Passive monitoring (just watching traffic, not interfering) reveals real usage patterns. Public IPs are fair game for security scanning under responsible disclosure principles.
368.po: First large-scale characterization of Starlink's ground infrastructure, revealing architectural choices, user behavior, and security posture without proprietary information.

369.bp: Chinese idioms are like colorful sayings in English ('raining cats and dogs')—the literal words (cats, dogs) don't explain the real meaning (heavy rain). Multimodal systems need to get this: the picture and text together should point to the idiom's true metaphorical sense, not just its surface words.
369.wh: An idiom's literal words and true meaning can be opposite. 'Kill two birds with one stone' sounds violent but means efficiency. Worse, the same idiom means different things in different contexts. Systems that just match words to images miss the metaphor entirely.
369.ap: The system builds a graph showing explicit relationships between literal and metaphorical meanings of each idiom. It also creates specialized sub-systems (experts) that understand different types of idioms—one for when literal and metaphorical meanings apply, one for when they diverge. Each expert focuses on its specialty; they vote to pick the best idiom.
369.ww: Explicit semantic graphs make metaphors tangible rather than hidden. Specialized experts divide the labor, so the system doesn't try to solve all idiom types the same way. Voting combines their knowledge.
369.po: System accurately selects idioms from image-text pairs, handling both the literal-to-metaphorical jump and context-dependent meanings better than systems that ignore metaphor.

370.bp: Language models now augment their answers by fetching real data from knowledge bases before answering. This is safer than hallucination—if the data is trustworthy. But what if attackers slip false information into the knowledge base? Systems need defenses.
370.wh: Graph-based knowledge systems reorganize raw text into structured graphs (entities, relationships) before retrieval. This should be safer than raw-text systems because structure filters noise. But attackers can also forge structure—fake relations, fake entities that look real—and mislead the model.
370.ap: The attacker creates poisoned 'toxic events' (fake facts disguised as real ones) and plants them in the knowledge base. They also fake the history of how these facts evolved from real information, making false knowledge seem like it legitimately evolved from seed facts. In multi-target attacks, they link poisons so they reinforce each other.
370.ww: Structured graphs look more trustworthy to models, so poisoned structure is more persuasive than raw text. Fake event evolution (showing false intermediate steps) makes invented facts seem like natural consequences of real knowledge.
370.po: Demonstrates vulnerabilities in graph-based knowledge systems; shows attackers can poison knowledge graphs more effectively than raw-text systems, revealing a security gap in retrieval-augmented systems.

371.bp: Graph neural networks learn from network structure (social graphs, citation graphs, molecule connections). Most treat the whole graph as one flat object. But real graphs hide internal organization—tight communities, bottleneck nodes—that matter for learning.
371.wh: Treating a graph as flat misses its internal structure. Some nodes act as bridges between communities; some are local hubs. Simple augmentation (randomly removing nodes) treats all removals equally, but destroying a bridge is much worse than removing a hub.
371.ap: Decompose the graph into tree-like structures (a classical graph theory tool) where local neighborhoods become 'bags.' Compute importance scores for each node and edge based on their role as bridges or hubs. Use these scores to make intelligent augmentation: preserve bridges, destroy isolated nodes, weaken global hubs. Also craft a new similarity loss that treats tree-based proximity differently from plain graph distance.
371.ww: Decomposition reveals hidden structure. Importance scores target augmentation intelligently—removing what matters most (bridges) hurts learning worse than random, so preserving them matters. Tree-based similarity captures topology that edge-based distance alone misses.
371.po: Graph learning (self-supervised and supervised) improves over state-of-the-art by respecting internal structure during augmentation and similarity computation.

372.bp: VTubers—digital avatars with human performers—are a multi-billion-dollar entertainment industry. But the business model is punishing: agencies own the persona, the performer bears all reputational risk, and when they quit and restart ('reincarnation'), they lose audience, income, and sometimes face harassment.
372.wh: Nobody has measured the cost of reincarnation at scale. Is it a minor blip or catastrophic? Without numbers, performers and agencies can't push for better contracts or industry reform.
372.ap: Researchers analyzed 12 major reincarnation cases using 728K livestream sessions and 4.5 billion viewer interactions, tracking metrics like audience size, revenue, harassment, and industry impact before and after reincarnation.
372.ww: Large-scale data reveals patterns individual cases might hide. Livestream metrics are objective (viewers can't lie), and social media interactions capture harassment quantitatively.
372.po: First empirical study proving reincarnation causes severe career damage to performers—substantial audience loss, income drop, increased harassment—with implications for labor practices and industry sustainability.

373.bp: Graph classification systems are trained on a fixed set of categories (e.g., 'toxic', 'safe'). But in the real world, new node types appear that the model never saw (novel classes). The system must either classify unknown nodes or reject them as 'unknown,' without retraining.
373.wh: Standard graph learning maximizes performance on known classes but doesn't build clear boundaries between known and unknown. Novel class nodes cluster randomly among known classes instead of being recognized as outliers. Existing methods don't handle mixing known and novel classes well.
373.ap: Novel 'negative Mixup' synthetically creates intermediate examples between known classes that push the model to learn clearer decision boundaries. Separate contrastive learning (training examples to be similar to their true class, different from others) maximizes spread between classes and compactness within classes, across multiple graph-processing layers.
373.ww: Negative Mixup creates hard cases at class boundaries, forcing the decision boundary to be clear and sharp rather than fuzzy. Multi-layer contrastive learning ensures that structure (how nodes connect) is consistent with class identity at every depth, making unknown nodes stand out as poorly-connected-to-any-class.
373.po: System reliably rejects novel class nodes while maintaining high accuracy on known classes, even when test data heavily mixes known and unknown categories.

374.bp: Live streaming platforms need real-time moderation and sentiment detection—flagging hate speech or sudden mood shifts instantly. But video, audio, and text streams arrive asynchronously and late, so systems must decide with partial information.
374.wh: The lightweight encoder learns by aligning audio/visual cues with text (cross-modal contrastive training). Loss down-weights examples where the target segment barely overlaps the frame, since those cases are too noisy to learn from reliably.
374.ap: Use a fast, lightweight streaming encoder for most frames. When a case is ambiguous or needs deeper understanding, route it to a heavyweight vision-language model. If context is insufficient (too early in a scene), defer the decision until more evidence arrives.
374.po: System achieves accuracy comparable to using vision-language models alone while calling the expensive model only occasionally, dramatically reducing latency and computation on live streams.
